Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to address the Human Rights Council for the first time as independent expert on the enjoyment of all human rights by older persons. I assumed this mandate on the 1st of May conscious of the responsibility entrusted to me and grateful for the important work of my predecessors. I have since participated in the first substantive session of the Intergovernmental Working Group on the Human Rights of Older Persons, and I look forward to its second session in October. I also thank the Government of Spain for inviting me to undertake my first country visit in November of this year. Mr. President, Today, I present the first report to the Council on cognitive impairment and the continuing exercise of human rights by older persons. At this pivotal moment of global aging, cognitive impairment is a phenomenon that grows increasingly frequent, touching the lives of many older persons and their families. The longer we live, the more different from one another we become, whether in health or other outcomes. Yet older age is still too often seen chiefly through vulnerability, dependency and decline. Once that lens takes hold, it can quietly shape expectations, services and even the way people are spoken to. My report asks what happens to the exercise of human rights by older persons when cognition changes and that change is met by ageism or assumptions of incapacity. While cognitive impairment is not confined to older age, it may carry particular human risks in later life. A diagnosis can begin to speak louder than the person. Others may assume that a voice counts less, that choices can be taken over, or that participation is no longer needed. I'm grateful to all those who contributed to this report. One message emerged clearly. Cognitive impairment does not diminish personhood, human agency, or entitlement to human rights. As a neurologist, I have spent much of my professional life with people whose memory, language, or ability to make complex decisions was changing. One lesson has stayed with me. What changes in the brain and what remains of the person are not the same question. A person may lose words and still express trust or refusal. Someone may need help with a decision and still have values, preferences and a life recognizably their own. The human rights problem begins when cognitive change is interpreted as loss of personhood, when diagnosis becomes a shortcut to incapacity, when an older person is spoken for rather than listened to, or when relationships and preferences are treated as if they had ceased to matter. Human rights do not become less universal when their exercise has become more difficult. That is precisely when their universality matters most and is most profoundly tested. International human right is a law is clear. Equal dignity, non-discrimination, recognition before the law, respect for will and preferences, participation and free and informed consent continue to apply. Where support is needed, it should help the person remain present in decisions about their own life. Autonomy is too often equated with complex independence, yet none of us lives autonomously in isolation. Throughout our lives, choices are made within relationships of care, trust and support. Cognitive impairment does not create this reality. It makes something fundamental about the human conditions more visible. In the right form, such support helps a person continue to shape their own life. This may require more time, familiar people, or adapted ways of communicating. Agency may be expressed in a gesture, a refusal, a habit, a look, or in a preference known over many years. Families, professionals, and institutions must learn to hear the forms in which a person can still speak. Participation is also made of ordinary choices. where to live, whom to see, how to spend a day, whether to go out, whom to trust. These are not small matters. Together, they make up a life. Mr. President, the enjoyment of human rights cannot depend solely on the goodwill of families, caregivers, or professionals. Families often provide indispensable support. that cannot relieve states and public systems of their own responsibilities. Those responsibilities must be translated into what I describe in the report as rights-realising systems. The responsibility of states must be visible in law and in everyday practice. States have positive obligations to create conditions in which older persons living with cognitive impairment can continue to exercise their rights to the greatest extent possible. Health and long-term care services should be organized around the person rather than the disease. Their success should be measured not only by clinical outcomes, but also by whether people retain meaningful influence over their own lives and relationships. In my report, I call on States to examine laws and practices that restrict rights on the basis of age, diagnosis or cognitive functioning. I also call for stronger support to decision-making and accessible communication, meaningful participation and inclusion, action against ageism and stigma, and effective monitoring and remedies when rights are denied. Older persons living with cognitive impairment must also have a place in shaping the policies and services that affect their enjoyment of human rights. Ultimately, the test is practical. Do laws and policies, institutions and everyday practices allow a person to continue to exercise their rights to the fullest extent possible as circumstances change and years pass? In short, Our task is to make sure that an older person's need for care and support when living with cognitive impairment never becomes a reason to see less of the person or to violate their enjoyment of human rights. I look forward to our dialogue and to hearing experiences and good practices of States and other stakeholders. I thank you very much, Mr. President.

Recently, China has paid in full its 2026 assessed contribution to the UN, contributing over 20 percent of UN finances. China practices what it preaches, including to support the UN-centered multilateral system. We cannot but ask, compared with a certain major country that refuses to pay its contribution, thereby exacerbating the financial crisis of the UN, hampering the normal functioning of the UN system, including the Council, why China's goodwill has not been cherished, but instead distorted and maligned? China has repeatedly reaffirmed that Taiwan, Xinjiang, Sichuan, and Hong Kong affairs are purely China's internal affairs. They concern China's sovereignty, security, and territorial integrity. The Chinese Government and people are best placed to speak on these issues, and this brooks no interference by any country or external forces. China is a unified multiethnic country, and the relations between ethnic groups are that of equality, unity, mutual assistance, and harmony. Enhancing the rule of law will help better protect the legitimate interests of all ethnic groups and enhance unity and promote joint development. We attach great importance to protecting the culture of ethnic minorities and the languages and the spoken language of ethnic groups. Our practices and achievements have been widely acknowledged and supported by the international community. We urge the NGOs to stop spreading false information and political maneuvering in order to play a positive rather than a negative role in international human rights cooperation. I thank you.

Thank you. This was the last speaker on my list. Is there any other delegation requesting to exercise right of reply in relation to the statements made today. I see no such request. We will now take a short break before holding the panel discussion on promoting and protecting economic, social and cultural rights within the context of addressing inequalities. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, we will now begin the panel discussion on promoting and protecting economic, social and cultural rights within the context of addressing inequalities, held pursuant to Council resolution 60/14. It is my honour to welcome to the podium Mr. Volker Turk, High Commissioner for Human Rights, who will deliver an opening statement. It is also my honor to welcome our distinguished panelists, His Excellency Mr. Gui Dejie, Permanent Representative of China to the UN Office in Geneva and other international organizations in Switzerland; Ms. Laura Chinchilla, President, Club de Madrid, who will deliver a video message; Ms. Penelope Hawkins, Head of the Debt and Development Finance Branch, United Nations Trade and Development; and Ms. Melissa Akir, Commissioner of the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia or SUHAKAM. Excellencies, distinguished participants, the list of speakers will close in 15 minutes. I encourage all speakers to intervene in an interactive way, present comments, and ask questions that reflects the panelists' intervention and the discussion. The speaking time limit is one minute and 30 seconds for all and a maximum of 40 speakers will be accommodated. Delegates inscribed on the list of speakers who cannot take the floor because of time constraints can upload their statements to the online system to be posted on the HRC portal. And I now have the honor to invite the High Commissioner for Human Rights to deliver the opening statement. You have the floor, sir.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished co-panelists and distinguished participants. Over the course of these weeks, this Council will hear about wars, repression and horrific violence. Our discussion today invites us to look at another kind of violence, and it's the countless quiet wars people endure every day in every part of the world against poverty, hunger and exclusion. These crises may differ in nature and scale, but beneath them runs a common cause, an insatiable competition for power, whether that is military, economic, political or technological. Over the past five years, about half of the world's countries have increased their military budgets. While every country has a duty to defend its people, it also has a duty to meet their essential needs. Increases in military spending often have direct consequences for education, housing, healthcare and social protection, and direct benefits for the military-industrial complex. Economic inequalities are soaring. the G20 Global Inequality Report found that since 2000, the richest 1% has captured 41% of new wealth and the poorest half of humanity, just 1%. In a world of trillionaires, more than one third of humanity lives perilously close to extreme poverty. A similar share lives in inadequate housing, and more than half fear losing their jobs. Our international economic and financial systems are grotesquely out of balance and in need of a major upgrade. Some 3.4 billion people live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on either health or education. Rising debt burdens combined with inequitable international tax rules, tax evasion and avoidance, and illicit financial flows leave many developing countries with virtually no fiscal space to provide basic services for their people. Least developed countries and countries affected by conflict and climate change are hit particularly hard. These funding gaps put people everywhere at risk. Underfunded health systems, for example, have made recent cholera and Ebola outbreaks harder to contain. Despite trillions being spent on advanced weaponry, few could credibly call the world I've just described secure. We are being sold an outdated, narrow vision of security which is more effective in protecting wealth than people. Mr. President, policies and choices that perpetuate poverty and inequality and fail to address the climate emergency are a form of oppression. Economic, social, and cultural rights are not merely about salaries. They are about freedom, agency, and autonomy, all of which are being steadily taken away from people. Extreme fortunes bring the ability to influence policy, direct public discourse, restrict competition, shape taxation, and shield controversial business models from public scrutiny. The same G20 report found that highly unequal countries are seven times more likely to experience democratic decline. My office's own data shows the growing suppression of civic space around the world, environmental defenders and journalists investigating corruption are often the first in the line of fire. Less transparency and undue restrictions on participation and peaceful protest are meant to close off ways for people to challenge unjust and corrupt systems. But those who impose them are building a dam. Unless they change course, That dam will eventually burst under growing pressure as people's grievances spill over into unrest. In many countries, people, especially young people, are already losing trust in their governments and taking to the streets. Mr. President, human rights are about redistribution of power. That is what makes them radical and threatening to those who would rather keep power to themselves. My office supports governments around the world in implementing inclusive policies that empower their people through education, opportunities, infrastructure, and more. An educated voter can participate more fully in public life. A digitally connected person can access information, services, and jobs. A woman with a secure income can be less dependent on an abusive partner. Empowered people make society stronger. And we have already seen it in many places around the world. Spain, for example, boasts social enterprises that employ thousands of people with disabilities and generate billions in profit. The country is now investing in its care and support system to promote autonomy and inclusion. In cities in Brazil and India, Greater participation has strengthened local governance, made policies more responsive, and reinforced accountability. We need a fundamental rethink of our economic approaches and systems to turn them towards fairness, equal participation, and human rights at every level. We need to wake up and stop pretending that economic models are working when they are destroying our environment, heating our climate, and fueling unsustainable consumption. We are running up an enormous debt to our planet and future generations, so it's really time to start paying it back. That is the basis of my office's work to promote sustainable economies that tackle inequalities and deliver for everyone. At a time of dwindling development aid, a human rights economy can help countries mobilize domestic resources through fair taxation, smarter spending, and more effective and transparent institutions. In Bangladesh, for example, we are supporting the tax reform process, including efforts to shift the tax towards more progressive taxation. We worked with civil society and media workers in Uzbekistan to strengthen their capacity to monitor and assess budgetary decisions. We need more cooperation, more political and financial support, more resolve and more creativity to take this work further. How wealth is distributed should be one of the key measures of economic progress. There is momentum at the international level which we need to leverage. I welcome initiatives to reform international financial institutions, to tax multinational corporations and high net worth individuals more effectively, to ensure developing countries have a seat at the table in debt discussions, to advance universal social protection, and to address climate-induced loss and damage. My office will continue working to ensure that the future UN tax convention has a strong human rights anchor. By working together, including through the Global Alliance for Human Rights, we can advance the human rights economy, and translate its principles into concrete policies and practices worldwide. I firmly believe this approach has the potential to deliver greater security and more sustainable prosperity than all the military might in the world combined. Thank you.
Thank you. I will now give the floor to the distinguished panelists for their initial presentations. And I give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Githa Gya. You have the floor, Excellency.

Distinguished High Commissioner, Mr. President, guests and colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. It's a great pleasure to to see the 60th anniversary of the International Covenant of Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, and see or attend the convening of the panel held pursuant to Human Rights Council Resolution 60/14 to discuss together progress, challenges, and opportunities in the field of economic, social, and cultural rights. China, together with other members of the core group, has introduced resolutions on the promotion and protection of economic, social, cultural rights in the context of addressing inequalities. Progress has been made in promoting cooperation in this field. First, panel discussions have been held at the Human Rights Council to pool ideas, build consensus, and inject fresh impetus into international cooperation on economic, social, cultural rights, ESCR rights. Second, a mandate was established for the creation of a new mechanism. The Knowledge Hub for Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, established by the Office of the High Commissioner, represents a major international institutional innovation and cooperation has been conducted with over 45 countries, effectively helping them strengthen their capacity. And the platform provides over 100 examples of good practices and 300 knowledge products to users worldwide. Third, international cooperation has been encouraged. China and OHCHR have jointly organized two training programs on ESCR. Representatives and experts from more than 40 countries in Asia, Africa, Latin America, and Oceania Participated in the training, which provided practice support for professional training and capacity building in the field, China, as a member, as a party to the International Covenant of ESR, attach great importance to the promotion protection of the rights and promoted progress in the protection, we fully… protected the adequate level for living standards of people and historically eliminated absolute poverty. We achieved the level goal 10 years ahead of schedule described in the 2030 agenda for sustainable development. We actually protected the ESR, right? The nine-year compulsory education have achieved to the extent of 91 percent. And the Higher education has achieved 61% coverage. We have the world's largest medical insurance coverage. The average life expectancy reached 79 years, and the right to health has been better protected. Over the next five years, guided by its fifth National Human Rights Action Plan, China will take further practical measures to safeguard economic, social, cultural rights, and the rights and interests of special groups. Not long ago, in his global update, the High Commissioner mentioned that only four years left before 2030 agenda has expired, only a small percentage have been achieved, economic, social, cultural rights have long been ignored. in the context of financial crisis in the UN, the financial allocation is not balanced and many people in the world are not able to fully exercise their rights, which exacerbated inequalities within and among countries. Given the above challenges, all parties should make efforts. We propose that country should place the realization of economic and social cultural rights at a higher level of priority on the multilateral agenda, and we should let people feel the difference that human rights make in their life and increase their confidence in. First, we should revitalize global cooperation, and all parties should honor their commitments under the Convention and reject marginalization of economic, social, cultural rights. We should meet the expectations of countries and vulnerable groups and reduce inequalities among countries. We call on developed countries to provide more technical and financial support to developing countries. Second, we should foster global governance and safeguard multilateralism and strengthen global human rights governance by increasing the representation of developing countries. and give due attention to their needs in the field of economic, social, cultural rights. We should uphold the right of people in all countries to independently choose their own paths of human rights development, oppose interference in internal affairs, and oppose unilateral coercive measures. Reform measures in the international human rights field must not result in disproportionate cuts to resources allocated to economic, social, cultural rights. We must achieve balance between two categories of human rights. Third, we must Third, we must enable HCHR to play its full role. We support the office in fully exercising its coordinating role in promoting protected rights. We have just heard the role that his office has already played in this regard. We support his office in further broadening the reach of the Knowledge Hub on economic, social, and cultural rights and providing a wider range of resources, guidance and tools, strengthen engagement with member states so as to provide targeted technical support based on their real needs. The office should also strengthen professional networks, establish regular cooperation with the universities and research institutions. China stands ready to continue to support through voluntary contributions. We are ready to work with all parties to continue advancing the equal and full exercise of economic, social and cultural rights by all. jointly steer global human rights governance in the right direction of healthy development of the international human rights cause. Thank you, sir.
Thank you. I now give the floor to Ms. Laura Chinchilla for a video message.

Thank you, President, High Commissioner, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. It's an honor for me to speak to you this afternoon as president of the Club de Madrid, the largest global organization bringing together former heads of states and government who were elected democratically, who share their experience and their leadership to promote inclusive, responsible, and people-centered democratic governance. From this perspective, we also approach economic, social, and cultural rights. Today, there is greater recognition that social protection, health, education, care, and access to water and sanitation are important. But there is a growing and increasingly growing gap between recognized rights and those rights which people actually enjoy. Figures show this clearly in 2024. 2.1 billion people, that is one in every four people on the planet, lacked access to drinking water safely managed. 3.4 billion did not have safe sanitation and 1.7 billion did not have basic sanitation services in their home. These gaps have deadly consequences. In 2019, at least 1.5 million people died because of preventable causes linked to unsafe water and deficient sanitation. And just in 2024, over 560,000 cases of cholera in 60 countries were reported. Structural inequalities, as well as discrimination, continue to condition the few opportunities that millions of people have extreme concentration of wealth, uh, attests to this reality in 2025, the 10% most wealthy in the world, uh, owned 75% of global, uh, wealth, whereas the… poorest 50% only owned 2% of global wealth. These gaps are not only economic in nature, they also affect our democracies. The Global Commission on Democracy and Multilateralism, which was set up by the Club de Madrid, underscores that economic, social and cultural rights are not merely outcomes of good governance. Rather, they are indispensable conditions for the full exercise of citizenship. Without economic, social and cultural security, democracy runs the risk of just becoming a mere formal exercise. We should also address the serious problem of corruption, which negatively impacts enjoyment of economic, social and cultural rights. For example, in the sector of health, corruption gives rise to greater avoidable mortality, lower immunization coverage, people paying more out of their own pocket, affecting the most vulnerable. Off-the-book payments, bribes, workplace absenteeism, institutional negligence and fraud contribute to health inequalities and act as health social determinants. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the other covenants and the other international human rights treaties remind us that human rights are indivisible. civil and political rights, economic, social and cultural rights, the right to development, the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. All of these together make it possible for effective democracy to take place and human development to take place. We cannot uphold some rights and neglect others. If states want to implement these principles, they need to have the real means to do so. The Club de Madrid has defended fairer, more predictable debt mechanisms, greater concessional and countercyclical financing, safer tax systems and more inclusive international financial governance. But to have resources is not enough either. What you need to do is translate these into effective rights and see social protection as an investment and It is the backbone of our democracies' infrastructure. In that respect, we must absolutely strengthen compliance with commitments under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and encourage states to consider ratification of the optional protocol to the ICESCR, given that many of the factors that condition the enjoyment of those rights transcend national borders and call for collective responses. All of this strengthens the importance of the multilateral system. More than ever, we need to bridge gaps between international commitments and the implementation of international commitments. This is exactly where the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights can, plays, or does play a fundamental role. As former heads of state and government, we know that to convert commitments in outcomes is one of the main challenges of governmental action. In the current context, where in which budgets are being cut, it's important that we preserve the capacity of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights to support states and to strengthen national capacities. You can rely on the Club de Madrid. We will continue to be an ally in this constant effort to keep economic, social and cultural rights at the heart of the global agenda and to ensure that their enjoyment is fully guaranteed and effectively enjoyed, that these rights are fully guaranteed and effectively enjoyed, which is essential if we want to create societies that are fairer and ensure that our democracies are sounder. Thank you very much.
Thank you. And I now give the floor to Ms. Penelope Hawkins. You have the floor, madam.

Thank you very much. At UNCTAD, we believe that public debt is an essential tool for development. And the problem is not debt itself, but indeed the conditions under which it was contracted and is being serviced. Increasingly, what we see in the developing world in particular is high borrowing costs and debt service obligations that are reducing the fiscal space available for governments to invest in the very areas that underpin economic, social, and cultural rights, particularly health, education, and essential public services. From a human rights perspective then, debt is not separate from the realization of these rights, as the cost of finance affects what governments are able to deliver to their people. I'd like to share with you a few of our recent findings. And one of the key things that underpins this in recent work we've done in the last couple of months is that debt is becoming more and more costly and less accessible as a source of development finance for developing countries. If one takes the span of two and a half decades between 2010 and 2025, you see that developing countries, excluding China, paid an average interest rate that was almost three times higher than that of the average paid by developed countries. So this trend over two decades is really showing us a systemic issue, and it reflects how markets and creditors assess the risks associated with developing countries. In 2025, developing countries paid almost US$1 trillion away in interest. This is just interest on public debt. This is not the repayment of debt itself. We see that 94 developing countries are paying such high rates that if they could access markets at the same rates as developed countries, they would save some 500 billion US dollars a year. I'll give you an example of what $500 billion a year can pay for. It can pay for 375,000 schools. It can pay for 1.6 billion children to be fed every day for a year. So we are not just talking, when we talk of interest, about financial cost. We are talking about opportunity cost, the resources that go into servicing interest on debts means that we have children that have to forego education or in fact undergo inadequate nutrition and/or inadequate health services. We see that between 2022 and 2024, developing countries excluding China transferred more resources to external public creditors than they received in financing. That simply means that all new debt or new loans, new financing, new investments that come into developing countries are being equal or exceeded by interest costs. So it seems that this external financing is no longer a reliable source for development. In the public sector, we can now say that 25 developing countries spend more on interest than education, and 49 spent more on interest than health. In total, in 2024, 3.7 billion people lived in developing countries where interest spending exceeded public spending on health and/or education. What we see at the same time, of course, is that other sources of external assistance for developing countries has fallen away. Official development assistance has fallen from 0.37% of combined gross national income from the Development Account Committee to 0.26% in 2025. all the time moving away from the UN target of 0.7% of GNI. So what is it that the UN can contribute? First of all, we believe that there is room for strengthened integration of debt and macroeconomic policy with human rights conditions and considerations. We believe that UNCTAD, working together with the Office of High Commission on Human Rights, could actually help develop more fulfilled and complete policies. Second, we believe that there is space always for continued technical assistance and national institutional capacity. UNCTAD's Debt Management and Financial Analysis System, also known as DMFAS, currently allows 65 countries to be enabled to produce sound debt management, debt data transparency, and institutional capacity. And in addition, we think that there is room to reinforce the UN's convening role to strengthen the voice of borrowers and facilitate peer learning. At the launch of the Borrowers' Platform in April this year, UNSG Guterres said, "I believe the creation of the Borrowers' Platform is an essential instrument in order for there to be change in power relations, and this change is essential for us to have fairness in the international financial architecture." If we work together, we can ensure that finance finance development on sustainable and affordable terms is not only possible, but can also support economic, social, and cultural rights. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor now to Ms. Melissa Aguirre. You have the floor, madam.

Thank you so much, Mr. President. It is a great honor to participate in this discussion today. As a commissioner of the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia, or SUHAKAM in Malay, I am especially pleased that this panel coincides with the 27th anniversary of SUHAKAM as an NHRI. For more than two decades, SUHAKAM has worked to promote and protect human rights in Malaysia through monitoring, investigation, human rights education and awareness, law and policy engagement, and cooperation with partners. So HAKAM has consistently recommended to the Malaysian government to accede to the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, henceforth ICESCR, including through studies on the compatibility with Malaysian laws. Last month, through the Asia Pacific Forum's high level dialogue, SOHAKAM has identified ICESCR as the most strategic priority for ratification. We sustain engagement with government institutions across Southeast Asia and crucial stakeholders to translate human rights standards and recommendations into concrete policies, institutional mechanisms, and improvements in the enjoyment of rights. However, as we have heard, in the context of human rights pushback, in a world where inequalities continue to deepen, despite significant advances in human rights standards and development, allow me to share a few key lessons from the Malaysian experience. First, progress on economic, social and cultural rights requires sustained engagement, clear evidence-based action, partnerships and institutional long-term commitment. One example in Malaysia concerns the right to health under Sustainable Development Goal 3, clean water and sanitation in places of detention, as well as addressing deaths in custody. Through monitoring, published research and sustained engagement with authorities, including with the Royal Malaysian Police and the Ministry of Health in Malaysia, our work contributed to the establishment of custodial health units within police lock-ups. While great challenges remain, this experience serves as a positive example of how sustained monitoring, evidence-based action, and constructive engagement with duty bearers can help transform a human rights concern into concrete institutional reform that improve the lives and dignity of all the rights holders affected. Secondly, economic and cultural rights through the National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights, or NAP-BHR, Far from being business as usual, since 2025, Suhakam was among the earliest institutions in Malaysia to advocate for this process, beginning with research on the human rights impact of business activities, including particularly in logging and plantation industries. The adoption of the NAP-BHR signifies Malaysia's commitment to integrating the UN Guiding Principles and Sustainable Development Goal targets into the national policy and governance framework. Crucially, the NAP-BHR recognises the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and highlights the need to institutionalise the principle of free, prior and informed consent in practice. Our experience with the NABHR has taught us that advancing rights is often a long-term process of sustained engagement, institutional continuity, and improved collaborations. Second lesson, that meaningful participation is essential to reducing inequalities and advancing human rights in a meaningful manner. This has guided SWACAM's work with indigenous peoples, particularly women, children, persons with disabilities and others facing discrimination and exclusion. Earlier this year, SWACHAM organised a national forum on the rights of indigenous peoples with the support of OHCHR. The discussions built upon the national inquiry into the land rights of Indigenous peoples, and reaffirm that customary land rights, the preservation of culture and identity, and participation in decision making are central to the overall well-being of Indigenous communities. A particular highlight was on cultural identity through the mapping and preservation of Indigenous oral tradition, storytelling, and languages. to preserve that and through the role of the state assemblies in Malaysia to preserve indigenous rights. As Suhakam is the chair of the Southeast Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum or CNF, we continue to nurture stronger strategic collaboration among Southeast Asian and HRIs to advance the rights of indigenous peoples, strengthen their communities, initiate monitoring of corruption and promote business practices that center indigenous rights and culture. Similarly, in our engagement on sexual and reproductive health rights and ending harmful practices, among others, with UNFPA, women and girls are not merely beneficiaries of policy decisions, but are active participants in shaping their rights in their daily lives. The same principles underpin our efforts to promote human rights cities in Malaysia. which have received support within the Department of Federal Territories. OHCHR's guidance and in-person support from the ESCR section have been useful for the promotion and strategic collaboration with Parliament, as well as the Malaysian Bar, followed by government officers under the Minister of the Federal Territories. We are excited to move forward with the state, with the support of HCHR, towards advancing human rights in the local government level and ultimately supporting the federal territories in becoming human rights cities. However, at the same time, significant challenges remain. Structural inequalities continue to affect access to healthcare, education, housing, land, social protection, and decent work. Indigenous peoples, women and girls, migrants, refugees and persons living in vulnerable situations continue to experience disproportionate barriers in their enjoyment of their rights. We are also witnessing increasing pressure on public resources and institutions tasked with protecting rights. In many countries, including across the Asia-Pacific region, human rights institutions navigating challenging circumstances, especially economically, as well as resource constraints. In this context, it is important to mention the unique value of collaboration between SWACAM and OHCHR. The relationship and engagement have been long-standing, particularly with the Regional Office for Southeast Asia and recently the ESR Knowledge Hub. So, Hakam will develop a context-specific ESCR monitoring tool with the technical support and collaboration of OHCHR to assess the government commitments towards fulfilling our human rights obligations. Let me end with a concrete recommendation. Greater investment is needed in national human rights institutions so that we fully comply with the Paris Principles. and HRIs are critical partners in monitoring implementation, generating evidence, supporting dialogue with authorities and the United Nations in order that the experience of rights holders truly inform public policy and contribute to regaining rights. At a time of widening inequalities, strengthening OHCHR's capacity to provide technical assistance and capacity development on ESCR is essential to supporting implementation on the ground. So, Hakam remains committed to explore collaborative opportunities towards substantive equality and amplifying the Paris principles to advance human rights for all. Thank you so much.

Thank you. Excellencies, distinguished representatives and members of the panel, we will now proceed with the first segment of the list of speakers. All interventions from the floor are limited to one minute and 30 seconds. The list of speakers is now closed. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iceland on behalf of a group of countries.

Mr. President, I have the honour to deliver the statement on behalf of the Nordic-Baltic States. We reaffirm that all human rights are universal and intertwined, and that economic, social, and cultural rights are central to leaving no one behind. We remain concerned by growing inequalities, which are further amplified by overlapping global crisis and their disproportionate effects on people in marginalized and vulnerable situations, including women and girls. Women and girls continue to face these barriers in access to equal pay, healthcare, education, and social protection. We stress the importance of nationally defined social protection floors and equal pay for work of equal value, which remains as one of the essential tools to close these gaps. In this context, the ongoing challenges and constraints faced by the Office of the High Commissioner are worrying, risking its capacity to deliver on its mandate. We reaffirm the need for predictable and adequate resourcing for the UN human rights pillar, including this Council and respectively OHCHR, to deliver its mandated work and underline the importance of gender balance and equitable geographical representation across its work. We look forward to continued cooperation with the Office and stakeholders to ensure economic, social and cultural rights frameworks deliver equally for all. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union.

Mr. President, the EU welcomes today's dialogue advancing the work of this Council on economic, social and cultural rights. The EU addresses economic, social and cultural rights and systemic inequalities by combining domestic legislative frameworks, intersectional equality strategies and human rights policies. Our Member States lead on a number of HRC resolutions in this area, such as the right on safe drinking water and sanitation, tabled at this Council session. Other resolutions are on key issues such as education, adequate housing, mental health, sustainable development and extreme poverty, as well as the omnibus resolution on the realization in all countries of economic, social and cultural rights. The EU follows a human rights-based approach to ensure that no one is left behind and that development is rights driven and transparent. Through the Global Gateway strategy, we promote public and private sustainable investment in building and strengthening health, education, and research. We commend the office for its work in this field and encourage the High Commissioner to continue his work. We appreciate that the knowledge hub on ESCRs has evolved into an interactive, practical tool for global use. Distinguished panelists, what main trends do you identify in successful rights-based national practices aiming at providing quality public services for the realization of economic, social, and cultural rights? Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Venezuela on behalf of a group of countries.

Gracias.

Thank you, Mr. President. We deliver a statement on behalf of the Group of Friends in Defence of the Charter of the United Nations. The Group of Friends reaffirms that all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated, and must be treated on an equal footing and with the same emphasis. In this context, the full realization of economic, social and cultural rights is an indispensable condition for ensuring human dignity, promoting social justice, and advancing towards more just and equitable societies. We note with deep concern the persistence and deepening of economic and social inequalities which affect millions of people and continue to manifest themselves both within our societies and in the profound gaps that persist between developed and developing countries. Overcoming these inequalities requires addressing their structural causes and advancing towards a more just. UCMs deepen inequalities and undermine the ability of States to guarantee full enjoyment of economic, social and cultural rights of their peoples. Thank you very much, Mr. President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of New Zealand on behalf of a group of countries.

Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of Australia, Canada, and my own country, New Zealand. All human rights, including economic, social, and cultural rights, are fundamental to building resilient and prosperous societies. They are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated, and apply to all without discrimination. One set of rights cannot be fully enjoyed without the other. The universal enjoyment of economic, social, and cultural rights faces persistent challenges, as we have heard from the panel. These include conflict and humanitarian crises, weak governance, and discrimination against marginalized groups. States bear the primary responsibility for fulfilling all human rights. Effective implementation of economic, social, and cultural rights requires practical solutions and measurable outcomes, the full, equal, and meaningful participation of all sectors of society, as well as evidence-based decision-making. Good governance and effective institutions are also vital. UN human rights mechanisms are key to supporting states to fulfill these rights through technical assistance and capacity building and in holding states to account. We call for predictable and sustainable funding for the human rights pillar and encourage states to support efficiency and rationalization efforts at the HRC. International cooperation remains critical to strengthening the realization of economic, social, and cultural rights for all. We welcome continued dialogue to improve outcomes and to strengthen accountability.

Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bahrain on behalf of the GCC.

Thank you. We reaffirm that all human rights are interrelated. Economic, social, and cultural rights are integral part of the human rights system. They deserve the same attention as civil and political rights. Mr. President, these rights are increasingly important in the face of inequalities and their roots, such as conflicts and climate change, as well as varying technological progress, we must help States to abide by their commitment and to fully implement these rights. In this context, we express our concern at the impact of financial restrictions on the human rights pillar and the response to requests for technological assistance. We must have equality in the distribution of resources. We reaffirm that coordination and cooperation cannot replace proper resources. Within the current situation, how can the OHCHR enhance cooperation with regional organizations to improve their capacity to respond to requests for technical assistance? Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kenya on behalf of the African group.

The Africa Group welcomes the convening of this important panel. Thank you, Mr. President. Economic, social, and cultural rights are not aspirational objectives. They are legally recognized human rights, indispensable to human dignity, equality, and sustainable development. Their effective enjoyment must remain at the center of international efforts to address inequalities. Across Africa, states have made important progress in advancing these rights. Nevertheless, significant inequalities persist within and between countries. These inequalities are reinforced by historical injustice, discriminatory structures, unequal access to finance, limited fiscal space, and gaps in infrastructure and technology. Women and girls, children, persons with disabilities, older persons, and persons living in poverty continue to face disproportionate barriers to the enjoyment of their rights. The continent is also confronting multiple and mutually reinforcing crises. Debt distress and high debt servicing costs are constraining public investment in essential services.
